title: Thais Buy Twice Global Average of Health Food and Drink
paragraphs: Consumers in Thailand are spending heavily on products designed to improve their health, purchasing specialty health food and drinks at more than twice the global rate, according to a new survey.

The findings come from PwC Thailand's Voice of the Consumer Survey 2026, titled "The Rise of Everyday Health," which questioned 501 consumers in the country. It found that 80% of Thai respondents had bought specialty health food and beverages in the past 12 months, compared with a global average of just 35%.

Thai consumers are also enthusiastic buyers of other health products. Some 71% said they had purchased vitamins, minerals or dietary supplements during the past year, and 79% said they take such products regularly. Meanwhile, a third had bought fitness equipment.
This trend looks set to continue. Asked what they planned to consume more of, 68% of respondents mentioned fresh fruit and vegetables, 49% said vitamins and supplements, and 44% said dairy products.

The survey suggests that Thai consumers have a range of motivations. Nearly half, 49%, said they wanted to live longer and improve their overall health, while the same proportion wanted to reduce stress and support their mental well-being. Another 45% said they wanted to improve their concentration and mental performance.

Concerns about food safety appear to be a major factor. A remarkable 91% of respondents said they were worried about chemicals and pesticide residues in food, and the same percentage expressed concern about environmental pollution. In addition, 87% were concerned about ultra-processed foods, and 77% were worried about microplastics.

Technology is also playing an increasingly important role. Around 63% of respondents said they had used artificial intelligence to obtain health or wellness advice, and 85% said they would be comfortable using AI for at least one aspect of managing their health, such as planning exercise or getting nutrition guidance. Furthermore, 80% said they would pay more for wearable health monitoring devices, provided the data was reliable enough to be used for medical purposes.

Sanicha Akarakittilap, the health industries leader at PwC Thailand, said that health is no longer a priority only when people are sick. Instead, according to Akarakittilap, it is becoming part of people's everyday choices and spending, and consumers are becoming more discerning.
